query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of niobium (Nb) to the HfZrTi high‐entropy alloy will improve its ductility and toughness by promoting a more ductile beta-phase formation and fine precipitate dispersion.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTi HEA in its original composition exhibits limited ductility and toughness under ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a dilute concentration (e.g., 1–5 at.%) of Nb to the base alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature mechanical testing and standard processing conditions (e.g., casting or powder metallurgy) typical for HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stabilized, ductile beta phase and/or fine coherent precipitates within the BCC matrix due to Nb’s role as a beta stabilizer.
generation.mechanism: Nb acts as a compatible alloying element (a subgroup V transition metal) that modifies the lattice distortions and electron concentration. This promotes dislocation mobility and activates transformation toughening and precipitation hardening mechanisms that together improve ductility and toughness without severely compromising the high-entropy effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in ductility (e.g., higher fracture strain in tensile tests) and improved toughness (e.g., better resistance to crack propagation) compared to the unalloyed HfZrTi HEA.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties of the pure HfZrTi HEA, which are known to be limited in ductility and toughness.
generation.boundary: Excessive Nb addition may lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases or disrupt the desirable high-entropy solid solution, counteracting any beneficial effects.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration range of Nb and the exact trade-offs with strength or other properties require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfZrTi-based HEA samples with varying Nb additions (e.g., 0%, 1%, 3%, and 5% atomic percentages) using an identical synthesis method. Process the alloys under the same conditions and perform mechanical testing (tensile and toughness tests) along with microstructural characterization (XRD, SEM, TEM) to identify phase formation.
measurements: Phase composition and morphology (via XRD and TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added alloys do not show statistically significant improvements in ductility and toughness over the baseline HfZrTi HEA or if Nb addition induces undesirable brittle phases or degradation of other critical properties, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
